exercise.title: Why does the tiny corner disappear in the limit?

statement.p: The exact change in a product includes the extra term \Delta f\,\Delta g. In your own words, why does that corner not survive in the derivative, and why does the argument need differentiability of the factors?

hint.p: A product of two small changes is smaller than first order. Differentiability implies continuity, so \Delta f\to 0 while the remaining difference quotient stays finite.

paragraphs.title: A hypothesis warning
paragraphs.p: The product rule says that if both factors are differentiable, then the product is differentiable. The converse is not true.
The factor |x| is not differentiable at 0, so the product rule cannot be used at 0. But F itself is differentiable at 0. Indeed,
So a product may have a derivative even when one factor does not. The rule gives a safe sufficient condition, not a complete test for every possible product.

exercise.title: Why is a quotient a product with a reciprocal?

statement.p: When a denominator increases, the reciprocal decreases, and the quotient rule follows by combining that fact with the product rule. In your own words, why does the minus sign appear, and why must we still require g(x)\neq 0?

hint.p: A larger denominator makes each output smaller. The reciprocal is undefined where the original function is zero.

exercise.title: Why does simplifying a quotient not define the missing point?

statement.p: For x\neq 1, the quotient \dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1} agrees with x+1, but the original function is not defined at x=1. In your own words, why can there be no derivative at a point where the function itself does not exist?

hint.p: Algebra can reveal nearby behavior. Differentiability still requires the function to have a value at the point.

warning.title: A quotient rule warning
warning.p: Simplifying a quotient can reveal nearby behavior, but it does not automatically define the missing point. Differentiability at a point requires the function to exist at that point.
